section_summary: This section combines records on the 1933 World Monetary and Economic Conference with memoranda on China, Japanese trade policy, and a possible oil monopoly. Later reports trace Japan’s budgets, trade controls, and economic capacity during the war in China, including conflicting assessments of its reserves and industrial output. The section ends partway through a 1938 report on economic conditions in western Japan.

subfiles.title: Conversations with Japanese representatives on the Monetary and Economic Conference
subfiles.about: American and Japanese delegates discuss tariff cooperation and trade barriers.
subfiles.summary: The delegates weigh a limited tariff truce, bilateral reductions, the 1927 Geneva convention, quotas, and most-favored-nation treatment. Afterward, the Japanese ambassador tells Hornbeck that the two delegations should stand together at the conference.

subfiles.title: Miscellaneous Memoranda
subfiles.about: Introduces a group of memoranda.
subfiles.summary: Divider for three memoranda.

subfiles.title: Viscount Ishii’s Attitude Toward the Integrity of China
subfiles.about: Ishii’s earlier statements are offered as background for talks about China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites Ishii’s memoirs and Japan’s 1904 correspondence recognizing Manchuria as part of China and supporting Chinese territorial integrity.

subfiles.title: Viscount Ishii’s Visit: Need of Caution
subfiles.about: Officials are advised to guard against later misinterpretation of conversations with Japanese representatives.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum rejects a claim that the Anglo-Japanese alliance had been revived and explains a narrower 1928 understanding about consultation over China. It cites disputed later interpretations of Roosevelt’s remarks and the Lansing–Ishii Agreement as grounds for care in the coming talks.

subfiles.title: Proposed Sale of Cotton to China
subfiles.about: A proposed American loan to China is assessed against the China Consortium Agreement.
subfiles.summary: The writer connects Japanese opposition to international reconstruction aid with its China policy. A unilateral American loan, it argues, could undermine the 1920 Consortium Agreement and reopen competitive financial diplomacy in China.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Oil Problem: Possible Monopoly or Governmental Control
subfiles.about: Introduces documents on Japanese oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Divider for records on oil monopoly and control proposals.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo telegram on Japanese oil plans
subfiles.about: Japan is considering an oil monopoly or import and refining licenses.
subfiles.summary: Press reports describe proposals that could displace foreign oil companies in Japan. The ambassador reports diplomatic approaches seeking clarity and asks whether the plans might conflict with commercial treaties.

subfiles.title: Table of Contents
subfiles.about: Lists the conference, China, and oil documents in the bundle.
subfiles.summary: Contents page naming memoranda, conversations, telegrams, and despatches.

subfiles.title: File note on Grew despatch of May 8, 1933
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on currency and Japanese export profits.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to reports that dollar inflation and yen appreciation reduced some exporters’ profits.

subfiles.title: Economic Legislation Passed by the Diet and General Economic Conditions
subfiles.about: Recent Japanese economic laws and financial conditions are summarized.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt covers steel consolidation, exchange and export controls, farm debt relief, and rice purchases. It then discusses dollar and yen movements, silk prices, tariffs, exchange rates, and the coming conference.

subfiles.title: File note on Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference
subfiles.about: Points to a report on the August 1933 Manchu-Japanese Economic Conference.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a conference report.

subfiles.title: File note on conversation with Japanese ambassador
subfiles.about: Points to a conversation about improvement in Japan’s economy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Phillips’s conversation with the Japanese ambassador.

subfiles.title: File note on labor conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to comments on Japanese living costs and labor conditions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference concerning cheap labor, long hours, and living costs.

subfiles.title: File note on Grew despatch 607
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch on Japanese manufacturers and industries.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a general economic conditions report.

subfiles.title: Miscellaneous Financial Notes
subfiles.about: Japanese silk, rayon, railways, crab exports, and shipbuilding are surveyed.
subfiles.summary: Silk sales to the United States have fallen while rayon profits and railway receipts have risen. Shipowners are buying foreign hulks to meet scrapping rules attached to construction subsidies.

subfiles.title: Received sheet
subfiles.about: Records receipt and routing of material.
subfiles.summary: Partly illegible receipt sheet.

subfiles.title: Confidential routing note to Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Far East Section, Division of Regional Information
subfiles.about: Forwards Williams’s confidential comments.
subfiles.summary: Suggests that Hornbeck read confidential comments from Williams.

subfiles.title: Pertinent Factors in Japanese Situation
subfiles.from: C. K. Moser, Far Eastern Section
subfiles.about: Digest of confidential commercial attaché reporting on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The digest reviews the Diet, deficit finance, rice purchases, textile competition, and trade talks with Britain and the Netherlands. It also considers oil barter, trade controls, and growing American purchases of Japanese sundries.

subfiles.title: File note on May 1934 business conditions
subfiles.about: Points to a résumé of Japanese business conditions in May 1934.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew’s business conditions report.

subfiles.title: May 1934 business conditions
subfiles.about: Briefly assesses the Japanese stock market and business climate.
subfiles.summary: Reports steady business, a firm but unsettled stock market, and caution amid a possible cabinet crisis.

subfiles.title: Request to return enclosure copy
subfiles.about: Requests the return of a detached despatch enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Office requests an enclosure copy for its records.

subfiles.title: Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a British report on Japan’s economy in 1933–1934.
subfiles.summary: Transmits three copies of a British trade department report.

subfiles.title: File note on Tokyo telegram 54
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram on Japan’s economy after the coup attempt.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to exchange, stock market, and cabinet uncertainty.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram 54 on financial conditions
subfiles.about: Reports economic conditions after the recent uprising.
subfiles.summary: Markets were disrupted, but banks and exchange rates remained relatively stable. Financial circles were anxious about the next cabinet and its finance minister.

subfiles.title: File note on “Japan In Suspense”
subfiles.about: Points to an article on Japan’s economic situation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a June 20 article in The Statist.

subfiles.title: Memorandum quoting Waring on Japanese prices
subfiles.about: Passes on observations about wartime prices and labor unrest.
subfiles.summary: Quotes Waring’s report that costs and prices had risen about 20 percent, with new labor unrest.

subfiles.title: Comment on “Economic Japan after Six Months of the China War”
subfiles.about: Assesses Coville’s account of Japan’s wartime economic resilience.
subfiles.summary: The reviewer accepts that Japan has so far borne the war’s economic burden, citing prior capital investment, military stocks, and raw materials. It warns that depleted reserves, falling exports, and rising living costs will shift the burden onto the public.

subfiles.title: Economic Japan after Six Months of the China War
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Examines Japan’s production, war costs, and ability to sustain fighting in China.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates Japan’s peacetime production and argues that years of military spending and capital investment enabled factories to redirect output to war needs. Gold financed advance purchases of war materials. Prices had risen, but daily life and consumption had changed relatively little after six months. The author concludes that Japan could bear a greater immediate war load while leaving its longer term capacity uncertain.

subfiles.title: File note on Bullitt’s Warsaw conversation
subfiles.about: Points to a conversation with Japan’s ambassador to Poland.
subfiles.summary: Notes Sakoh’s fear of economic collapse if the war continued six more months.

subfiles.title: Comment on Tokyo despatch 2813
subfiles.about: Flags Yoshino’s remarks and disputes an explanation of Japanese bond flotation.
subfiles.summary: Recommends reading the Yoshino conversation and notes disagreement over Williams’s interpretation of limited bond issues.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Economic Position, and Other Matters
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits confidential memoranda on Yoshino’s economic views.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards the Yoshino conversation and the commercial attaché’s comments, requesting restricted distribution.

subfiles.title: Conversation between Yoshino, Parker and Meyer
subfiles.about: Yoshino discusses Japanese controls, war planning, and foreign capital.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino defends import and exchange controls as preparation for a prolonged emergency. He describes Japan’s economic adaptability, criticizes British assessments, and suggests that foreign capital may be welcome in North China.

subfiles.title: Williams memorandum to Dooman
subfiles.about: Williams evaluates Yoshino’s claims about Japan’s economic capacity.
subfiles.summary: Williams supports strict exchange control but questions Japan’s ability to expand munitions output. He says Sansom shares that concern and doubts that American capital will soon fund development in North China or Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Comment on “Economic Trends in Western Japan”
subfiles.about: Recommends selected passages of a Kobe economic despatch.
subfiles.summary: Calls the despatch lengthy but occasionally informative.

subfiles.title: Economic Trends in Western Japan
subfiles.about: Surveys foreign commerce, domestic trade, prices, and employment in western Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report finds a sharp decline in 1938 exports, especially to the United States, while warning that customs figures omit some war imports. Import controls and wartime demand have raised domestic prices and profits, drawing goods from export markets. Domestic business remains active, and the excerpt reports little immediate unemployment, though it anticipates possible difficulty after demobilization.
